doc.title: James Moody — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Only Black musician in the Hilton house band
summary: The orchestra was white with a few Mexican players; Moody was the lone Black member, and he says it is about how one carries oneself.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Now, the groups the -- the house band, for example, the house orchestra at the Las Vegas Hilton where you were, these were mixed bands.
Mixed -- white musicians and black musicians -­
-- all in the same band or no?
No. Let me see. There was a guy by the name of Willie -- I forgot what Willie's last

name was. Willie was a Negro, but in this band -- in this band, they wanted somebody Negro in there, but -- but they didn't seem to be able to get one, but just before I -- I left, there was a guy -­ what was his name? Rudy? -- Rudy or something. He had been in the Air Force band. He got a job there then everything folded. But I was the only -- only so-called, you know.
I was wondering about that because it seemed to me in -- much in the same way as the Hollywood Studios were at that time -­
-- that that was a scene that wasn't real open.

No, no, see, because first of all, you see, it was security and it's always like that, you know, when you go places, most places where there's a job with security, I mean, you might have a token there, but other than that -­

-- it's for the -- it's for the, like -- like -- like Redd Foxx said, "It's for God and three other white men." You know. [laughter] You know. So, like, you know what I'm saying? So that, but -- but I was the only -- I was -- the whole band was Caucasian with a couple of Mexican gentlemen and I was the only Negro in there. And they had females in there, you know, playing strings along with the guys and everybody was -- everybody was wonderful.
You know, then again, it's the way you carry yourself, you know. You are what you are. But, you know, I'm proud of what I am, you know?
